Alright. First topic today. Why do you forget almost everything you learn? Here's a number that should bother you. In the eighteen eighties, a German psychologist named Hermann Ebbinghaus sat down and memorized long lists of nonsense syllables. Words like dax, bok, and yat. Then he tested himself at different intervals to see how much he still remembered. What he found became known as the forgetting curve. Most of what he learned was gone within a day. Not some of it. Most of it. And the steepest drop happened in the first hour.

Now, you might say, well, those were nonsense syllables. Real information is different. And you'd be partly right. Meaningful material sticks better. But the shape of the curve shows up again and again. You learn something, you feel confident, and then it quietly drains away while you sleep.

The good news is that Ebbinghaus also found the fix. Every time he reviewed a list, the curve got flatter. The memory lasted longer. And if he spaced those reviews out, waiting a little longer each time, he needed far fewer total repetitions to lock the list in. That's called the spacing effect, and it is one of the most reliable findings in all of psychology.

So here's the practical version. When you learn something you actually want to keep, review it the same evening. Then again two days later. Then a week later. Then a month later. Four short reviews will beat one long cramming session almost every time. Cramming feels productive because the information is fresh in your head. But fresh is not the same as stored.

Second topic. And this one is for anyone who has ever felt guilty about how much time they spend on their phone. Last spring I ran a little experiment on myself. For thirty days, I deleted every social app from my phone. Not blocked. Deleted. I kept messages, maps, and the camera. That's it.

The first three days were honestly embarrassing. I picked up my phone, unlocked it, stared at the home screen, and put it back down. Over and over. I counted one afternoon and I did it forty one times in about four hours. My thumb was going to places that no longer existed.

By the end of the first week, something changed. The reaching stopped. And what replaced it was not productivity, which is what I expected. It was boredom. Long, flat, uncomfortable boredom. Waiting in line at the pharmacy with nothing to look at. Sitting on the bus just watching the street.

And here's the part I did not see coming. Somewhere in the second week, the boredom started turning into ideas. I'd be standing at a crosswalk and suddenly figure out how to fix a problem I'd been stuck on for a month. Three of the episodes you've heard this year came out of that thirty days. Your brain needs empty time to connect things. When every gap gets filled, the connecting never happens.

When the thirty days ended, I reinstalled exactly one app. And I moved it off my home screen into a folder on the last page. That tiny bit of friction cut my use by more than half. I didn't need more willpower. I just needed the thing to be slightly harder to reach.

Okay, third topic. Let's talk about food that refuses to go bad. Archaeologists excavating ancient Egyptian tombs have reported finding pots of honey that were thousands of years old. And the honey was still edible. Thousands of years. Meanwhile the bread in my kitchen goes green in five days.

So why does honey last forever? Three reasons, and they stack. First, honey is extremely low in water and extremely high in sugar. Bacteria that land in it get the water pulled right out of them. They basically dry out and die. Second, honey is acidic. Most microbes hate acid. Third, and this is the cool one, bees add an enzyme to the nectar that slowly produces small amounts of hydrogen peroxide. So honey has its own built-in disinfectant.

There's one catch. If you let water get into the jar, all bets are off. That's why honey that's been stored badly can ferment. Keep the lid on, keep it dry, and your honey might outlive you. Honestly, it might outlive all of us.

Here's a quick bonus fact while we're in the kitchen, because I cannot stop thinking about it. Botanically speaking, a banana is a berry. And a strawberry is not. A berry, in the botanical sense, is a fruit that develops from a single flower with a single ovary, with the seeds inside. Bananas, grapes, tomatoes, and even eggplants all qualify. Strawberries don't, because their seeds are on the outside and the fleshy part grows from the base of the flower, not the ovary. So the next time someone at dinner says they love berries, you can ruin the meal with that.

Fourth topic. And I want to slow down for this one, because it changed how I think about money. Imagine you put away one hundred dollars a month. Just one hundred. And imagine it grows at around seven percent a year, which is roughly what a broad stock market fund has returned over long stretches of history, though nothing is guaranteed and the past does not promise the future. If you do that for forty years, you will have put in forty eight thousand dollars of your own money. But the account would be worth somewhere around two hundred and sixty thousand dollars.

Read that again in your head. You put in forty eight thousand. The other two hundred thousand or so came from growth on top of growth. That's compound interest, and the reason it feels like magic is that our brains think in straight lines. We imagine money growing like a staircase, one step at a time. It actually grows like a snowball rolling downhill.

The flip side is brutal, though. If you wait ten years to start, and do the exact same thing for thirty years instead of forty, you don't end up with three quarters of the money. You end up with roughly half. The last ten years are where the snowball is biggest. Time is the ingredient you cannot buy back. And please, this is not financial advice, talk to someone qualified about your own situation.

Fifth topic, and this is my favorite animal fact of all time. An octopus has three hearts. Two of them pump blood through the gills, and the third pumps it around the rest of the body. And here's the strange part. When an octopus swims, that third heart actually stops beating. Which is one reason octopuses prefer crawling to swimming. Swimming literally exhausts them.

Their blood is also blue. Not a little bit blue. Properly blue. That's because instead of using iron to carry oxygen, like we do, they use copper. Copper-based blood works better in cold water with little oxygen, which is exactly where a lot of octopuses live.

And then there are the arms. Around two thirds of an octopus's neurons are not in its head at all. They're in its arms. Each arm can taste, touch, and make simple decisions on its own. Researchers have watched a severed octopus arm keep reaching for food and try to pass it toward where the mouth would have been. So when you see an octopus solving a puzzle, you're watching something closer to a committee than a single brain.

Sixth topic, and it's a short one, but it's the one I get the most messages about. The two minute rule. It's simple. If a task will take less than two minutes, do it right now. Don't write it down. Don't add it to a list. Don't think about whether it's important. Just do it.

Reply to the short email. Put the dish in the dishwasher. Hang up the coat. The reason this works is not that the tasks are important. It's that the tracking is expensive. Every little undone thing sits in the back of your mind and costs you a tiny bit of attention. Fifty tiny costs add up to a day where you feel exhausted without having done anything big.

But, and this is the part people miss, the rule has a second half. If a task takes longer than two minutes, you are not allowed to just start it on impulse. You have to decide when. Otherwise the two minute rule turns into a way of avoiding your real work by doing a hundred small things instead. I know because I did exactly that for most of a year.

Seventh topic. Try this right now if you can. Reach up and tickle the palm of your own hand. Nothing, right? Maybe a faint itch. Now imagine someone else doing exactly the same movement. Completely different. So why can't you tickle yourself?

The answer lives in a part of the brain called the cerebellum, at the back of your head. Every time you move, your brain sends a copy of the movement command to the cerebellum, which predicts what that movement is going to feel like. When the touch arrives and it matches the prediction, the brain turns the volume down. It's essentially saying, relax, that was just us.

Researchers tested this with a clever machine. People moved a lever, and a robot arm tickled their palm with a soft piece of foam. When the robot copied their movement instantly, it barely tickled. But when the researchers added a tiny delay, just a fraction of a second, or rotated the direction a little, suddenly it started to tickle. The prediction was off, so the brain stopped filtering it out.

And here's the strange twist. Some people with certain conditions that affect how the brain tags its own actions can actually tickle themselves. Their prediction system doesn't label the movement as their own. Which tells you something wild. The feeling of being you, of knowing which actions are yours, is something your brain is quietly calculating every second of the day.

Eighth topic. Let me tell you about the worst job interview I have ever had. I was twenty three, I had one good shirt, and I had spent the entire night before memorizing answers to every question I could find online. Greatest weakness. Where do you see yourself in five years. All of it.

I walk in, I sit down, and the interviewer doesn't ask me a single one of those questions. Instead she slides a stapler across the table and says, sell me this stapler. I froze. I had nothing. So I did the only thing I could think of. I started describing the stapler. It's grey. It staples. It has a nice weight to it.

She let me go on for maybe forty seconds, which felt like a week, and then she stopped me and asked, how many staplers do you think this office goes through in a year? And I said, I have no idea. And she said, exactly. You never asked me a single question. You tried to sell me something without knowing anything about what I need.

I did not get that job. But that sentence has stayed with me for more than ten years. Every good pitch, every good conversation, every good piece of advice starts with a question about the other person. I just had to embarrass myself in a grey office to learn it.

Ninth topic. A few of you sent in questions, so let's do a quick round. Someone asked, do you actually read all the messages? Yes, I do. Slowly, but I do. Someone else asked what microphone I use. It's a fairly ordinary dynamic microphone, nothing fancy, and honestly the room matters more than the mic. Hang some blankets, close the curtains, and you'll sound better than any upgrade could make you.

And the best question this month came from a listener who asked, what's one habit that actually stuck for you? My answer is boring, and I think that's the point. I write down three things I did that day before bed. Not things I'm grateful for, not goals. Just three things I did. It takes about a minute. And on the days when I feel like I accomplished nothing, the list proves me wrong. It turns out most of my bad days are not bad. They're just forgotten.

Tenth topic. You've probably heard that playing Mozart to babies makes them smarter. There are CDs, there are toys, there was even a governor in the United States who proposed giving every newborn in his state a classical music recording. So where did this come from?

It started with a short paper in nineteen ninety three. College students listened to ten minutes of a Mozart sonata, then did a spatial reasoning task, the kind where you imagine folding a piece of paper and cutting it. They did a little better than students who sat in silence. The effect lasted roughly fifteen minutes. That's it. Not babies. Not intelligence. Fifteen minutes of slightly better paper folding in adults.

Then the headlines took over. The study became the Mozart effect, and the Mozart effect became make your baby a genius. Later researchers tried to repeat it and mostly found that any music people enjoy, or even an exciting story, gives a similar small, temporary bump. It's about being alert and in a good mood, not about Mozart. So play your kids Mozart if you love Mozart. Just don't expect it to do their homework.

I bring this up because it's the perfect example of how a small, careful finding turns into a giant, careless claim. The study wasn't wrong. The telephone game around it was. Whenever you read a headline that sounds too good, ask what was actually measured, in whom, and for how long.

Eleventh topic, and it's a story. A few years ago I got completely lost in Tokyo. My phone had died, it was close to midnight, and every street in that neighborhood looked identical. Narrow lanes, vending machines, little restaurants with their shutters down. I walked in circles for almost an hour.

Eventually I went into a tiny convenience store and tried to ask for directions, using about six words of Japanese and a lot of pointing. The man behind the counter listened, frowned at my hotel's name, and then did something I will never forget. He locked the store. He put up a little sign, walked out with me, and guided me for fifteen minutes through those lanes until we were standing at the hotel door. Then he bowed, turned around, and walked back.

I didn't have the words to thank him properly. I still think about that a lot. He didn't help because it was efficient or because anyone was watching. He just decided that a lost stranger was more important than his next fifteen minutes. I try to remember that whenever someone asks me for directions now, even when I'm in a hurry. Especially when I'm in a hurry.

Twelfth and final topic, and I'm ending on something that sounds like a riddle. Why do we fall asleep faster when someone reads to us? There's a decent explanation. When you lie in bed alone, your mind tends to wander toward the future. Tomorrow's meeting. The bill you forgot. The awkward thing you said in two thousand fourteen. That kind of planning and worrying keeps your brain alert.

A calm voice telling a simple story gives your mind somewhere else to go. It's interesting enough to stop the worrying, but not so interesting that you need to stay awake for it. That's the sweet spot. And it's why so many people fall asleep to podcasts, including, I suspect, some of you right now. If that's you, that's fine. I'm honored.
